My reporting indicates that while the Chinese don't want to talk about nuclear weapons, and they don't want to talk about long-range missiles, they're very willing to talk about artificial intelligence in part because they want the same thing we should want, which is stability. They want a stable state, and AI threatens all sorts of upheaval. People in cybersecurity will tell you the fastest way to know the capability of software is a penetration test, basically, where you see what a model can do, you test it in all sorts of ways, you see if you can break the model, and if you can, you send it back to the model maker and say this is not acceptable.I did a lot of reporting on the EU regulations. And historically, the EU has kind of been famous for over-regulating. And in this instance, I think they have a really good plan. They split regulations into model size, basically. So if you're running a chat bot on a restaurant review site, you're probably fine. If you're running a large language model that's aiming to create artificial general intelligence, you're going to be heavily regulated on the outputs of that model, knowing much more about what that model was trained on. You might even have regulators working with you in your offices. By the way, we do that for finance, right? Every major bank in the United States has regulators who sit there in the office because we realize that not knowing what risk we have can create large financial consequences and crises. I don't suggest that I have the answer or anybody has the answer. One thing I would say is we don't need all the answers to get some of them, and so we might want to start getting moving before this gets away from us.GROSS: If you're just joining us, my guest is Josh Tyrangiel. He's a staff writer at The Atlantic where he wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll be right back after a break. This is FRESH AIR.(SOUNDBITE OF SAINT SINNA SONG, "REAL FLOW")GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story, and it's about the space race between Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk. It's titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." He's also the author of the book "AI For Good."You write that AI and the unemployment and economic disruption it's going to cause are likely to be different than anything in the past, in part because the speed of change with AI leaves no time to adapt. Can you talk about that a little bit more?TYRANGIEL: Yeah. So when I was reporting the story just about AI and employment, there's a split in the ranks of economists. About half the economists I spoke to said, you know, look, AI is a general-purpose technology, and if you look at the steam engine, everybody thought that was immediately going to change everything, and it took 40 years to roll out. And the longer a technology takes to roll out, the easier it is for us to adapt to it. And there's a natural rate of adjustment in labor. You know, there's a reason that, over 30 years, we probably didn't notice that toll takers went away, that elevator operators went away. That took a long time to roll out. You lose 3% of a job category every year, and guess what? Thirty years later, it's gone without any real pain. We adapt.Then there's a younger set of economists, and these are ones who are much more vociferous about the fact that the older economists aren't misreading the data, they're just misreading the tech, and that AI is technology that has the capability to roll itself out. It's software that can create software, which means it could be massively accelerated. And so they're much more concerned that whether this takes five years, 10 years or 15 years, that's not 40 years. And if it takes any one of those numbers, our ability to adjust with compromised institutions of government and systems is going to be a crisis. They all acknowledge that the data doesn't show it yet, but they want us to be more prepared. And so that was the schism I found in the world of economy.GROSS: It's surprising that Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon agree on something, and what they agree on is that AI needs to be regulated. But I think they have some disagreements about what should be done to regulate it. What are they disagreeing on?TYRANGIEL: Well, this is very strange to say, but, you know, Bernie Sanders believes that there should be government representation on these boards, that there should be all sorts of remedies for potential AI job loss, that there should be a robot tax. And when I was reporting and talking to Steve Bannon about what Bernie Sanders was suggesting, Bannon said, I don't think he goes far enough. I think the government should have a significant piece of all of these companies. We should have board oversight, and we should be taking a profit from it. And I said, isn't that nationalization? And Bannon said, yeah, and some of the Republicans may hate me for it, but I believe that's where this is going and we have to get these companies under control. He went further than Bernie Sanders did on the need to socialize, effectively, these AI labs.GROSS: And you're right that Bannon thinks that Trump's decision to have the federal government take a nearly 10% stake in Intel was really brilliant.TYRANGIEL: Yeah, listen, I think that sometimes Bannon uses the press to speak to the president. And in this instance, where there's a tremendous distance between Bannon's position and Trump's position, I think he can be very coy about the president's responsibility with an AI. One of the things, you know, he told me, and I kept challenging him on, I said, well, the president disagrees with you so clearly. What are you going to do about that? He said, oh, he's just getting bad advice. It's - the people around him aren't giving him good advice. He's so smart, he'll figure this out.But clearly, there's massive distance there. And if you're a politician of any kind and you see that distance between someone who's a pretty important leader of the far right of the Republican Party and a Republican president, you'd be smart to co-opt it and use it to get what you want. And I think that's what Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon have figured out is that this is really important to both of them, and they're going to use everything in their power to create the pressure on the middle to make this happen.GROSS: Well, Josh Tyrangiel, thank you so much for talking with us.TYRANGIEL: It's - this was really my pleasure. Thank you so much, Terry.GROSS: Josh Tyrangiel is a staff writer for The Atlantic. His November cover story is titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos."
